title: Explore the ratings month by month
prompt:
The recommendations team wants features that describe each member and each film. They all come from the `ratings` export below: 4,704 rows, one per time a member rated a film. Look at it first. Add `ratings.printSchema()` and `print(ratings.count())` to your file and press Run.

Then write `ratings_by_month(ratings)`, one row per month, so you can see how much there is to learn from and when it happened. Count every row as it comes, repeats included: the next step cleans them.
rules: `month` is the month of `rated_at` as text, like `2026-03`.
`ratings` is how many rows fall in the month; `members` and `films` are how many different `user_id` and `movie_id` values they have.
`average_rating` is the mean `rating` of the month's rows, rounded to 2 decimals.
Every row counts, repeated rows included. Return `month`, `ratings`, `members`, `films` and `average_rating`.
hints: `F.date_format("rated_at", "yyyy-MM")` turns a timestamp into its month. Capital `MM` is the month; small `mm` is minutes.
Group by that month with `groupBy(...)` and compute all four numbers in one `agg(...)`.
`F.countDistinct("user_id")` counts members once each; `F.count("*")` counts rows. Round the mean with `F.round(F.avg("rating"), 2)`.
explanation: One `groupBy` on the month text gives one row per month, and one `agg` computes all four numbers in a single pass. `countDistinct` counts each member and film once, however often they rate, while `count("*")` counts the raw rows, repeats and re-ratings included. The table shows two things the rest of the project depends on: ratings grow fast towards the end of the export, and the dates run long enough to train on the past and check on the most recent months.
